142.title: The Passover at Jerusalem
142.b0.ask: “How is the one long known as a God of wrath revealed as a loving Father who assures us that we are his sons?”
142.b2.p: In Paper 141 Jesus and the twelve came down the Jordan valley and entered Jerusalem together for the first time. Now Paper 142 shows the month they spent in Jerusalem around the Passover. They worked in the city by day and slept at Bethany at night. From time to time Jesus stayed at the home of Flavius, a Greek Jew, where prominent Jews came to see him in secret.
142.b3.p: On the first day Jesus called on his old friend Annas, the former high priest, but was received coldly. As he left he said, “⟦Q 142:0.2⟧Fear is man’s chief enslaver and pride his great weakness.⟦/Q⟧” The paper goes on to teaching in the temple, a question about the wrath of God, the growth of the concept of God, the meeting with Nicodemus, and the relation of God and man seen in the light of the family.
142.b4.p: How, then, does the God of wrath spoken of by the old prophets connect with the loving Father Jesus proclaimed? And how can we be sure that we are that Father’s children?
142.b5.q: “⟦Q 142:5.2⟧If you receive God as your Father, then indeed and in truth are you the sons of God.⟦/Q⟧”
142.b8.p: Throughout this month either Jesus or one of the apostles taught in the temple every day, and when the crowds were too large, they held meetings outside the temple courts. Their message can be summed up in four points.
142.b9.t: The kingdom of heaven is at hand
By faith in the fatherhood of God one becomes his son
Supreme devotion to God, and loving your neighbor as yourself
Obedience to the Father’s will, bearing the fruits of the spirit
142.b10.p: Interested people among the Passover crowds carried this message to distant parts of the Roman Empire and to the East. In this way the gospel of the kingdom began to spread into the outside world, and Jesus’ work was no longer confined to Palestine.
142.b12.p: Jacob, a wealthy merchant from Crete, asked how it could be that Moses and the prophets called Yahweh a jealous God of wrath, while Jesus taught a merciful Father who loves all men. Jesus answered that the Father in Paradise is changeless, but that the concept of his nature had grown from the days of Moses through Amos and on to Isaiah.
142.b13.p: Jacob was the father of six children, and Jesus used them as an illustration. When young children are punished, they may think their father is angry; but when they grow up, they should see the love behind his discipline. So too mankind, as the centuries pass, should better understand the true character of the Father; there is no profit in successive generations of spiritual light if we keep seeing God as Moses and the prophets saw him. Jacob believed and asked to be led into the kingdom.
142.b14.q: “⟦Q 142:2.2⟧A good and true father not only loves his family as a whole—as a family—but he also truly loves and affectionately cares for each individual member.⟦/Q⟧”
142.b16.p: That night Jesus taught the apostles how the idea of God had evolved among the Jewish people. The Father in heaven never refuses the sincere worship of his children, however crude their idea of Deity or whatever name they call him by.
142.b17.t: The god of the Sinaitic clans, exalted by Moses as the Lord God of Israel
El Elyon, proclaimed by Melchizedek to Abraham
The God of heaven, learned in Egypt
A concept of the Trinity handed down from the days of Adam
In Isaiah’s day, the almighty and merciful Creator of the universe
A religion in which the believer becomes a son of God
142.b18.p: Jesus pointed out that the scriptures themselves show this growth. The book of Samuel says the anger of the Lord moved David, but a later record no longer laid the evil at Yahweh’s door and said instead that Satan had moved him. Understanding of the law grew in the same way.
142.b19.t: Centered on the unleavened bread, the first fruits, and rules of sacrifice
The new ten commandments of Sinai
Moral commandments fitting the enlarged concept of Yahweh
The positive law of love — to love God and one’s neighbor
142.b21.p: Flavius was a proselyte of the gate, neither circumcised nor baptized, and he had filled his home with sculptures and works of art collected from all over the world. He feared that the images would offend Jesus, but Jesus admired every room and asked many questions.
142.b22.p: Jesus said there was no reason to rebuke the enjoyment of beauty created by the Father and fashioned by the hands of men. Moses was right, in his day, to fight against idolatry, but now the children of Moses were making a false god of that very prohibition. In the coming kingdom men would not be told “thou shalt not do this”; they would set their hearts on one supreme duty — to worship the Father truly and to serve their fellows in love. Flavius believed and was baptized by John’s disciples.
142.b24.p: A man from Damascus asked how he could be sure that Jesus was sent from God and that he himself could truly enter the kingdom. Jesus answered that no worthy father would keep his son anxious about his place in the family. Neither does the Father in heaven leave his faith children in doubt.
142.b25.p: The Supreme Spirit bears witness with our spirits that we are the children of God, and whoever is born of the spirit has within himself the power to overcome all doubt. And the evidence to all the world that we have been born of the spirit is that we sincerely love one another.
142.b26.q: ⟦Q 142:5.3⟧Whosoever has been born of the spirit has in himself the power to overcome all doubt, and this is the victory that overcomes all uncertainty, even your faith.⟦/Q⟧
142.b28.p: Nicodemus, a wealthy older member of the Sanhedrin, afraid of being seen, came to Jesus by night at the home of Flavius. Jesus showed him no special deference, made no excessive effort to win him, and used no sarcasm; he treated him with calm dignity. He told him that unless a man is born from above — born of the spirit — he cannot enter the kingdom of God, and he likened the spirit to the wind.
142.b29.p: When Nicodemus asked how he could lay hold of this spirit, Jesus answered that the spirit of the Father already lived in him; by the wholehearted choice of its leading, he would be born of the spirit. Nicodemus had fine moral qualities, but he did not know how to submit his will to the Father’s will. Even so, he developed enough faith that later, when the disciples had fled, he joined Joseph of Arimathea in asking for the body of Jesus.
142.b30.t: Like the wind: its effects are seen, but the spirit itself is not discerned
By the wholehearted choice of the spirit’s guidance
142.b32.p: After Passover week Thomas asked how people should live once the kingdom had come, and what would become of slaves, property, law, and justice. Jesus explained that the kingdom of heaven is an evolutionary experience, beginning on earth and continuing up to Paradise. Men of other ages, he said, would better understand the gospel if it were put in terms of the family — the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man — rather than in terms of a kingdom. Then he described seven foundations of a true family.
142.b33.t: Children are born of their parents and inherit their traits
He delights to provide not only for their needs but for their enjoyment
He carefully prepares them for later responsibilities
He provides guidance and correction for immature children
He always listens and shares their difficulties
He forgives freely; he is no judge, enemy, or creditor
He leaves an inheritance, and the family goes on from generation to generation
142.b34.p: When Thomas said that the Father did not always seem merciful and that prayers were not always answered, Jesus told him to understand that this kingdom and its Father are spiritual. The earthly family is only an illustration; he begged them not to apply the teaching of the spiritual kingdom literally to worldly matters such as slavery, poverty, land, and human justice.
142.b36.p: At the end of April, as the opposition of the Pharisees and Sadducees grew plain, Jesus and the apostles spent the month of May working quietly from house to house in Bethlehem and Hebron. With Abner, Jesus visited the Nazarite colony at Engedi; many believed, but most would not accept him because he did not teach fasting and self-denial. The people of this region did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.
142.b37.p: In June they camped in the garden of Gethsemane and did no public teaching. One Friday evening Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came to see Jesus, but in their fear they turned back at the door of the tent. At the end of June, when Simon, a member of the Sanhedrin, openly espoused Jesus’ cause, a new movement to arrest him arose, and Jesus decided to withdraw to Samaria and the Decapolis.
142.b39.p: Paper 142 shows that it was not God who changed but man’s understanding of God that grew. From the god of the clans at Sinai to the merciful Creator of Isaiah, and now in Jesus, God is revealed as a Father who loves each person. Just as grown children come to see love in the discipline of their early years, so mankind must look past a God of wrath to see the Father. That Father leaves none of his children in uncertainty, and those born of the spirit already carry within them the power to overcome doubt. The evidence of it is a life of sincere love for one another.
142.b40.t: Through the Passover crowds the gospel began to spread to the outside world
The Father is changeless; the concept of him has grown
The idea of God evolved from Yahweh to the Father in heaven
Enjoying beauty is not to be confused with worship
The Father does not leave his children in uncertainty
Choosing the spirit’s guidance, one is born from above
The relation of God and man is that of a father and his children
Quiet personal ministry went on in the face of opposition
142.b42.box: God is not a God of wrath but a loving Father who keeps his children in assurance, and by faith we become his sons.
143.title: Going Through Samaria
143.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus first reveal who he was in Samaria, a land regarded as an enemy — and to a woman?”
143.b2.p: In Paper 142 we followed Jesus’ teaching in Jerusalem at the time of the Passover. Now Paper 143 begins on the road out of that city. At the end of June, A.D. 27, as the opposition of the Jewish religious leaders grew fierce, Jesus and the twelve left their tents and belongings at the home of Lazarus in Bethany and set out north toward Samaria.
143.b3.p: The people of southern Samaria heard Jesus gladly, and the apostles, except Judas Iscariot, overcame much of their prejudice against the Samaritans. The paper unfolds an objection raised in the gentile cities and Jesus’ impassioned reply, teaching on self-mastery and on rest, a woman met at Jacob’s well, and teaching on prayer and worship on Mount Gerizim.
143.b4.p: In a land that had been hostile for more than six hundred years, how did Jesus lead his apostles past their prejudices and offer living water to the hearts of the people?
143.b5.q: “⟦Q 143:1.4⟧Love is the greatest of all spirit realities. Truth is a liberating revelation, but love is the supreme relationship.⟦/Q⟧”
143.b8.p: In the first half of August the apostles had their first experience of preaching almost entirely to gentiles, in the Greek cities of Archelais and Phasaelis near the Jordan. The objection Philip reported was sharp. Greeks and Romans said this teaching was fit only for weaklings and slaves, and that it would turn men into feeble nonresisters who would soon vanish from the earth.
143.b9.p: Jesus answered with rare strong feeling. Even divine love has its severe disciplines, he said, and the Father rules a universe of universes by the compelling power of his love. The gospel must be carried alike to Jew and gentile, rich and poor, free and bond, and the service of the kingdom is no easy work — it calls for all the courageous manhood they can muster. From that day the apostles’ message took on a new note of courageous boldness.
143.b10.t: A higher type of human courage
Uncompromising loyalty to enlightened convictions — the highest courage
143.b11.q: ⟦Q 143:1.4⟧The ultimate goal of human progress is the reverent recognition of the fatherhood of God and the loving materialization of the brotherhood of man.⟦/Q⟧
143.b13.p: Jesus was a perfect example of self-mastery. He did not return insult for insult, and when he was criticized, he committed himself to the Father’s judgment. When Andrew asked how John’s self-denial differed from Jesus’ self-control, Jesus answered that John’s way was a religion of self-examination and self-denial, but that he had brought a new message of self-forgetfulness and self-control. He who rules his own self is greater than he who captures a city.
143.b14.t: First being changed by the Spirit of Truth
Faith and the rebirth of the spirit
143.b15.p: Jesus pointed out that men blame evil on the evil one when often they have simply been led astray by their own natural tendencies. The secret of self-mastery is bound up with faith in the indwelling spirit, which works by love — and even that faith is the gift of God. Those born of the spirit spontaneously bear the fruits of the spirit in daily life, and that is true self-mastery.
143.b17.p: By this time the apostles were worn out by conflicts with John’s disciples and by their contacts with gentiles and Samaritans. When Andrew came to Jesus nearly at his wit’s end, Jesus did not step into the tangled personal problems; instead he proposed three days of rest on Mount Sartaba. Andrew went to each man in turn and asked him not to speak of his troubles during the holiday.
143.b18.p: On the mountain Jesus taught that sometimes the best way to solve a tangled problem is to get away from it for a while; after resting, we can attack it with a clearer head. The next day they spent talking of things that had nothing to do with religion, and Jesus even left out the thanksgiving at the noon meal. When they came down after three days, they found that many of their problems had been the product of exaggerated fear and anxiety and had solved themselves while they were away.
143.b19.t: Condition on the way up the mountain
His head was full of problems
Hard pressed for funds among the gentiles
A periodic attack of sensitiveness and selfishness
Torn between patriotism and love of brotherhood
Bewildered by the way things were going
In the midst of a severe time of depression
143.b21.p: Jews and Samaritans had been enemies for more than six hundred years. The root went back to about 700 B.C., when Sargon, king of Assyria, carried away more than twenty-five thousand people of northern Israel and settled other peoples in their place. Religious hostility began after the return from exile, when the Samaritans hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Their temple on Mount Gerizim, built with Alexander’s permission, was later destroyed by John Hyrcanus.
143.b22.t: Sargon carried off the people of the northern kingdom and settled foreigners there
The Samaritans hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem
As a reward for their help, the Samaritans were allowed a temple on Mount Gerizim
John Hyrcanus destroyed the temple on Mount Gerizim
143.b23.p: The apostles had not minded preaching in the gentile cities, but the words “⟦Q 143:4.3⟧Let us go into Samaria⟦/Q⟧” put their loyalty to a severe test. Yet the personal loyalty they had built up in more than a year with Jesus proved stronger than their prejudice against the Samaritans.
143.b25.p: At Jacob’s well the weary Jesus asked Nalda, a woman of Sychar who had come to draw water, for a drink. In those days it was thought improper for a Jewish man to speak to a woman in public, let alone a Samaritan, so Nalda was greatly surprised. Jesus told her that whoever drinks this water will thirst again, but the water of the living spirit becomes a well springing up even to eternal life.
143.b26.p: Nalda misread Jesus’ kindness, but when Jesus told her to go and get her husband, she was brought to her senses. The book explains that her husband had unjustly divorced her, leaving her in a desperate position. She tried to sidestep the question of her own salvation by turning to the dispute over the place of worship, but Jesus answered that true worshipers worship the Father in spirit and in truth. When she spoke of the one who was to come, Jesus said, “⟦Q 143:5.7⟧I who speak to you am he.⟦/Q⟧” This was the first open declaration of his divinity and sonship he had made on earth.
143.b27.q: “⟦Q 143:5.6⟧God is spirit, and they who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.⟦/Q⟧”
143.b28.p: Leaving her water pot behind, Nalda ran back to the city and brought the people out to the well. The apostles were shocked, but Jesus taught that even a woman of doubtful morals has a soul that can choose God as its Father and so become his daughter. The narrative adds that the world should be more interested in the happy life of Jesus, which revealed God, than in his sad death.
143.b30.p: When the crowd came, the apostles urged Jesus to eat first. But he said, “⟦Q 143:6.1⟧My meat is to do the will of Him who sent me,⟦/Q⟧” and told them that the fields were already white for the harvest. Others — John the Baptist — had labored there, and now the apostles were entering into their labor to reap.
143.b31.p: On the first night on Mount Gerizim the apostles expected a rebuke, but Jesus did not mention the matter; instead he taught them about “the central realities of the kingdom of God.” He wanted all men to see God as a Father-friend, and he stressed again and again that love is the greatest relationship in the universe. The work in Samaria, which lasted until the end of August, prepared the ground for the remarkable work Philip later did in this region.
143.b33.p: At the evening gatherings on Mount Gerizim, Jesus taught that true religion is the act of an individual soul in its self-conscious relations with the Creator, while organized religion is man’s attempt to socialize that worship. Life is made healthy by a balance of things that complement each other.
143.b35.t: To help us think less but realize more
To look to the One for inspiration to serve the many
143.b36.p: Worship is the act of a part identifying itself with the Whole, the finite with the Infinite, the son with the Father. The apostles understood only part of this teaching, but, the narrator says, other worlds have understood it, and other generations on earth will.
143.b38.p: Paper 143 is a journey in which Jesus crosses the boundaries of prejudice one after another. Before the scorn of the gentiles, he showed that love is not weakness but the highest courage. To his weary apostles he taught not self-denial but self-mastery and rest in the spirit. And in a land of six hundred years of hostility, he first revealed who he was to a woman whom others looked down on most. At the center of that meeting was neither a place nor a doctrine, but worship in spirit and in truth and the living water received into the heart.
143.b39.t: The gospel of love calls not for weakness but for the highest courage
The self is mastered not by self-denial but by faith in the spirit
Sometimes stepping away to rest is the way to solve a tangled problem
Personal loyalty to Jesus was stronger than six centuries of hostility
To a rejected woman he first revealed who he was
The fields are white for harvest; love is the greatest relationship
Prayer sustains; worship is divinely creative
143.b41.box: God is spirit: what saves us is not a place but worship in spirit and in truth, and the living water received into the heart.
144.title: At Gilboa and in the Decapolis
144.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus teach that prayer is not a set form of words but the breath of the soul — and why did he let the two apostolic groups learn to reach agreement on their own?”
144.b2.p: In Paper 143 we saw Jesus and his apostles cross the boundaries of prejudice as they passed through Samaria. Now Paper 144 takes us into a time of retreat, in September and October of A.D. 27, at a secluded camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa.
144.b3.p: The leaders at Jerusalem were hostile, Herod still held John in prison, and tension was growing between John’s disciples and Jesus’ apostles. Jesus knew that the days of preparation were nearly over, but he did not want the next step to bring pain to John. So he decided first to train his apostles, and then to work quietly in the Decapolis until John’s fate was settled.
144.b4.p: What did Jesus teach his apostles in this quiet time? And how did the followers of John and of Jesus come to be one?
144.b5.q: ⟦Q 144:4.9⟧Prayer is a part of the divine plan for making over that which is into that which ought to be.⟦/Q⟧
144.b8.p: The apostles’ devotion was growing day by day, but it came mainly from personal loyalty, not from a full understanding of Jesus’ teaching and nature. Jesus made plain his three reasons for this retreat.
144.b9.t: To strengthen their understanding of and faith in the gospel of the kingdom
To allow the opposition in Judea and Galilee to quiet down
To see what would become of John the Baptist
144.b10.p: The apostles felt that their next public work would mark the beginning of the proclamation of the kingdom, but each had his own idea of what that kingdom would be. Jesus spent much of his time alone in the mountains in personal communion with the Father, and all through September prayer and worship were the center of their discussions. At last Thomas asked: “⟦Q 144:1.9⟧Master, teach us how to pray.⟦/Q⟧”
144.b11.t: The kingdom had not yet come
144.b13.p: Jesus first recalled the short prayer John had taught, explaining that it was meant for the people at large, not as a set form for expressing one’s own soul. Prayer is the personal and spontaneous expression of the soul’s attitude toward the spirit; it is the communion of sonship.
144.b14.q: “⟦Q 144:2.3⟧Prayer is the breath of the soul and should lead you to be persistent in your attempt to ascertain the Father’s will.⟦/Q⟧”
144.b15.p: With the story of the friend who goes at midnight to borrow bread, and of the widow who kept coming back, Jesus encouraged persistence in prayer. But persistence is not meant to change a just Father; it is meant to change our earthly attitude and enlarge the soul’s capacity to receive the spirit. And even when his children ask foolishly, the Father gives them good things with a parent’s wisdom.
144.b17.p: When James asked for a prayer to teach new believers, Jesus gave them the one he had taught his brothers and sisters at Nazareth. It begins “⟦Q 144:3.3|100:7.16|137:4.6⟧Our Father who is in heaven⟦/Q⟧” and includes petitions that our souls be refreshed with the water of life and that we be made more and more like him. Later, in the copying, two lines were lost and a closing doxology was added.
144.b18.p: Jesus was reluctant to pray in public, and he always taught the apostles to pray in secret. What he taught was not a form for personal prayer but a pattern for group, family, and social praying. Even when he prayed all night in the hills, he prayed mostly for his disciples and very seldom for himself.
144.b19.t: In submission to the Father’s all-wise will
144.b21.p: The earnest, longing repetition of a petition, when it is the sincere expression of a child of God uttered in faith, never fails to expand the soul’s capacity for spiritual receptivity — however ill-advised or impossible of direct answer the prayer may be. And in all praying we must remember that sonship is a gift. Righteousness is earned through progressive character development, but sonship is received by grace and through faith.
144.b22.t: Recharging the spiritual batteries of the soul
Tuning the soul to the universe broadcasts of the Father’s spirit
The breath of spiritual life in the midst of material civilization
A process of exchanging the human will for the divine will
144.b23.p: Peter, James, and John spent long nights with Jesus and yet heard very little of his praying, because most of his prayer took place silently, in spirit and in mind. Jesus usually prayed in the plural, not the singular, and only in the great crises of his life did he pray for himself.
144.b25.p: Jesus told the apostles about many other forms of prayer to illustrate other points, but asked them not to teach these “parables of prayer” to the multitudes. Many of these prayers came from other inhabited planets. By special permission, seven sample prayers are set down in this record.
144.b26.t: Our Father, in whom consist the universe realms
Give us the vivifying forces of light
Our creative Parent, who is in the center of the universe
Lead us by your own hand through the uncertain maze of life
Our perfect and righteous heavenly Father
Ever lead us in the ways of eternal progress
Our Father, who is in mystery
Bestow upon us the full mastery of self
Father and Mother, in one parent
Let our charity enfold the weak of the realm
The all-faithful Source and all-powerful Center
Refresh us day by day with the living waters
Our Father, who dwells in the secret places of the universe
Forget us not as we so often forget you
144.b27.p: The apostles were not free to teach these prayers publicly, but they gained much from them in their personal religious experience. All seven point in the end the same way: not our will but yours, and more and more like you.
144.b29.p: Early in October a chance meeting in a market led Jesus’ apostles and John’s twelve apostles to hold a joint conference at Gilboa lasting three weeks. Jesus firmly refused to take part in the discussions. He said that he was the Father’s representative to the individual, not to groups, and that they must decide for themselves the problems of socializing religion; then he was away for two weeks.
144.b30.t: To adopt the prayer Jesus had taught for instructing believers
Each group to carry on its own work, with a week of joint council every three months
Only John’s apostles would baptize; Jesus’ apostles would teach
John’s apostles would follow Jesus’ direction
Jesus’ apostles would begin water baptism as the emblem of the baptism of the Spirit
144.b31.p: John’s apostles preached, “⟦Q 144:6.9|134:9.8|135:7.3⟧Repent and be baptized⟦/Q⟧”; Jesus’ apostles proclaimed, “⟦Q 144:6.9⟧Believe and be baptized.⟦/Q⟧” This was the first attempt by Jesus’ followers to socialize personal religion. The twenty-four men learned to differ, to debate, to pray, and to compromise — and still to sympathize with one another’s point of view. When Jesus returned, he promised to support the spirit of their decisions.
144.b33.p: In November and December Jesus and the twenty-four worked quietly in the Greek cities of the Decapolis, such as Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara. The socialized religion of a new revelation always pays the price of compromise with the forms of the older religion; the price paid to bring John’s followers along was baptism.
144.b34.p: The two apostolic groups went out in pairs, John’s apostles baptizing and Jesus’ apostles teaching. John’s apostles at first believed in Jesus because of John’s testimony, but they soon came to believe through their own contact with Jesus and his teaching. Their leader, Abner, later became the head of the seventy teachers.
144.b36.p: At the end of December, while Jesus was teaching near Pella, John — now a year and a half in prison — sent messengers to ask: “⟦Q 144:8.2⟧Are you truly the Deliverer, or shall we look for another?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus had them tell John that he was not forgotten and that the gospel was being preached to the poor. To the crowd he said that John was no reed shaken by the wind, but more than a prophet.
144.b37.q: “⟦Q 144:8.4⟧Among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist; yet he who is but small in the kingdom of heaven is greater⟦/Q⟧”
144.b38.p: The reason is that even the least in the kingdom knows that he has been born of the spirit and has become a son of God. Through this event the two groups of followers truly became one, and John was greatly comforted when he heard the news. Jesus likened the generation that accepted neither John nor himself to children in the market place, and he promised rest to all who labor and are heavy laden.
144.b40.p: John the Baptist was executed by order of Herod Antipas on the evening of January 10, A.D. 28. His disciples took his body and buried it at Sebaste. When Jesus heard the news, he said to the twenty-four: “⟦Q 144:9.1⟧The hour has come to proclaim the kingdom openly and with power. Tomorrow we go into Galilee.⟦/Q⟧” On the morning of January 13 they set out for Capernaum.
144.b42.p: Paper 144 is the quiet time of preparation before the storm. At Gilboa Jesus taught prayer not as a fixed form of words but as the breath of the soul toward the Father, and he showed that persistence does not change God but enlarges our souls. At the same time, in the matter of the two apostolic groups he stepped back, letting them learn to debate, to compromise, and to bear with one another on their own. And just when the followers of John and of Jesus had become one, John passed away, and the time had come to proclaim the kingdom openly.
144.b43.t: In retreat, the apostles asked to be taught how to pray
Prayer is the breath of the soul; persistence enlarges the soul
Jesus taught secret, unselfish, social prayer
Sonship is a gift; prayer exchanges the human will for the divine
All seven sample prayers ask to become more like the Father
Without Jesus they reached agreement and learned tolerance
At the price of baptism, the two groups worked together
The least in the kingdom is greater than John
With John’s death came the time for open proclamation
144.b45.box: Prayer is not a word that changes God but the breath of the soul that changes us toward the Father’s will.
145.title: Four Eventful Days at Capernaum
145.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus, after healing hundreds in a single evening, turn away from the rejoicing crowd and leave Capernaum?”
145.b2.p: At the close of Paper 144, after John the Baptist had been put to death, Jesus declared that the time had come to proclaim the kingdom openly. Paper 145 picks up right after that. On the evening of Tuesday, January 13, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles arrived in Capernaum and, as usual, made their headquarters at the home of Zebedee in Bethsaida. From Wednesday through Friday Jesus taught the apostles, preparing them for their first extensive public preaching tour.
145.b3.p: Late on Friday evening his baby sister, Ruth, paid him a secret visit, and they spent almost an hour together in a boat anchored near the shore. Of all Jesus’ family, Ruth alone believed in the divinity of his earth mission consistently and unwaveringly, from first to last.
145.b4.p: Over these four days Capernaum saw an astonishing catch of fish, a memorable sermon in the synagogue, and a healing at sundown unlike anything before or since. Yet at the very moment when everyone was celebrating, Jesus did not rejoice; he left. Why?
145.b5.q: “⟦Q 145:4.2⟧Rejoice not that my Father is powerful to heal the body, but rather that he is mighty to save the soul.⟦/Q⟧”
145.b8.p: On Friday morning the crowd pressed Jesus so close to the water’s edge that he got into a boat and went on teaching for more than two hours. The boat was the “Simon,” Peter’s former fishing vessel, built by Jesus’ own hands. When he had finished, he told David Zebedee and his partners, who had fished all night and caught nothing, to put out into the deep and let down their nets. They took so many fish that all three boats nearly sank. From that day these men left their nets and followed Jesus.
145.b9.p: But the paper states plainly that this was in no sense a miracle. Jesus was a close student of nature and an experienced fisherman; he simply knew where the fish were usually found at that time of day. His followers, however, always regarded it as a miracle.
145.b11.p: On the Sabbath afternoon Jesus preached in the synagogue on “⟦Q 145:2.1|0:5.10|1:3.6⟧The Will of the Father in Heaven.⟦/Q⟧” His point was that religion is a personal experience. As a group they were the children of Israel, he said, but as individuals each one of them was a child of God — and God loves every one of them as an individual. This, he reminded them, was a truth Jeremiah and Ezekiel had already foreseen.
145.b12.t: God loves you — every one of you
The fathers eat sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge
All souls are God’s; each answers for himself
145.b13.p: God will not punish a nation for the sin of one person, Jesus said, nor punish one of his believing children for the sins of a nation — though members of a family often share the material consequences of the family’s mistakes. The hope of a better world is bound up in the progress and enlightenment of the individual. Once man discerns this spiritual freedom, the Father wills that his children begin the eternal ascent to Paradise in response to the urge of the indwelling spirit. Through this sermon the apostles grasped more fully that the gospel is a message to the individual, not to the nation, and the people were astonished, for he taught as one having authority and not as the scribes.
145.b14.p: As he finished, a young man in the congregation was seized with a violent epileptic attack and cried out. Jesus took him by the hand and said, “⟦Q 145:2.12⟧Come out of it,⟦/Q⟧” and he awoke. The paper explains that he was not possessed by a demon at all; he suffered from ordinary epilepsy, and he was not cured at that moment. Likewise, the fever of Peter’s mother-in-law, Amatha, happened to leave her while Jesus was at her side. Both were coincidences, but a wonder-seeking people spread them abroad as miracles.
145.b16.p: Jewish teaching did not permit anyone even to go in search of health during the Sabbath, so as soon as the sun went down, the sick began streaming toward Zebedee’s house. That afternoon Jesus had closed his sermon with words his hearers could not forget: “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Hate is the shadow of fear; revenge the mask of cowardice,⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Man is the son of God, not a child of the devil.⟦/Q⟧” Now almost a thousand people stood at the door.
145.b17.p: Jesus knew he could never build an enduring spiritual movement on material wonders, yet this suffering multitude deeply moved his heart. He placed the decision in his Father’s hands: if it were the Father’s will, he said, he would desire to see his children made whole. At that moment a vast company of celestial beings descended into the crowd, and 683 men, women, and children were perfectly healed. No one was more surprised than Jesus himself, and no such mass healing ever happened again in his earth life.
145.b18.q: ⟦Q 145:3.11⟧What a Creator Son desires and his Father wills IS.⟦/Q⟧
145.b19.t: What the sundown healing left behind
It spread through Galilee, Judea, and beyond; Herod sent watchers
From then on he was as much a physician as a preacher
Most of those healed were not permanently benefited spiritually
Such wonders were not part of the plan, only an incidental result
145.b20.p: The paper makes clear that these healing wonders were not part of Jesus’ plan for proclaiming the kingdom. On the contrary, they caused him much trouble, bringing prejudice-raising publicity and unwanted notoriety.
145.b22.p: That evening the apostles’ hopes soared higher than ever. From a human standpoint it was probably the greatest day of all their days with Jesus, and their lingering doubts were swept away. Only days before, near the borders of Samaria, Jesus had told them the hour had come to proclaim the kingdom in power — surely this was it. If this was only the beginning, what wonders lay ahead?
145.b23.p: But Jesus, deeply perturbed, had withdrawn. Those who had been healed waited late into the night to thank him, but he did not appear. When at last he returned, he refused their congratulations and adoration and said only that they should rejoice not in the healing of the body but in the saving of the soul. The twelve went to bed disappointed and bewildered; except for the twins, few of them slept much. One thought filled their minds: “⟦Q 145:4.3⟧We cannot understand him.⟦/Q⟧”
145.b25.p: Jesus hardly slept that night either. He saw the danger that caring for the sick might take up all his time and push aside his mission of establishing the spiritual kingdom in the hearts of men. Long before daybreak he went out alone and prayed for wisdom, so that human sympathy joined with divine mercy would not lead him to neglect the spiritual for the physical. Peter, James, and John found him, and for more than four hours he tried to explain — but they could not comprehend his teaching.
145.b26.t: Everyone is seeking you — come back and minister to them
My mission is to reveal the Father and proclaim the kingdom
Welcome the crowds that have gathered
They have come for the healing of their bodies, not for truth
A thousand could have been baptized
I must not become engrossed in healing to the exclusion of my teaching
145.b27.p: Jesus told Andrew he would not go back and sent him to prepare for the journey to the other cities of Galilee. On the afternoon of Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, the first public preaching tour began. The apostles followed reluctantly, until Thomas roused them: “⟦Q 145:5.10⟧We follow a teacher who seeks no glory for himself.⟦/Q⟧”
145.b29.p: Paper 145 shows the most stirring four days of Jesus’ life on earth. The catch of fish and the events at the synagogue were coincidences that people spread as miracles, while at sundown 683 people really were made whole in a single moment. Yet at the height of it all Jesus stepped back. The healing of bodies flowed from his mercy, but it could not build a spiritual kingdom in human hearts. So he chose the road to the next town over the cheering crowd, and remained a teacher who sought no glory for himself.
145.b30.t: The great catch was no miracle but the knowledge of a skilled fisherman
Religion belongs not to a nation but to personal experience
683 were healed, yet the kingdom does not rest on miracles
Rejoice not in the healing of the body but in the saving of the soul
Jesus turned from acclaim and set out to preach the gospel
145.b32.q: ⟦Q 145:5.4⟧the kingdom of the Father could not be built upon wonder-working and physical healing⟦/Q⟧
146.title: First Preaching Tour of Galilee
146.b0.ask: “In Galilean towns that were waiting for miracles, why did Jesus teach prayer, assurance, and love instead of giving signs?”
146.b2.p: In Paper 145 Jesus turned his back on the acclaim that followed the sundown healing and left Capernaum. Paper 146 is the record of the first public preaching tour of Galilee that began that day. For about two months, from January 18 to March 17, A.D. 28, Jesus and the twelve, assisted by the former apostles of John, preached and taught in Rimmon, Jotapata, Ramah, Zebulun, Iron, Gischala, Chorazin, Madon, Cana, Nain, and Endor.
146.b3.p: This was the first time Jesus let his associates preach without restraint. He cautioned them only to stay away from Nazareth and to be discreet in Capernaum and Tiberias, and the apostles threw themselves with great joy into preaching the gospel, ministering to the sick, and baptizing believers.
146.b4.p: Yet wherever they went, people expected miracles. What did Jesus teach in the midst of all this, and how did he deal with the events people called miracles?
146.b5.q: ⟦Q 146:2.8⟧Prayer does not change the divine attitude toward man, but it does change man’s attitude toward the changeless Father.⟦/Q⟧
146.b8.p: Rimmon had once been dedicated to Ramman, a Babylonian god of the air, and its people still held many Babylonian and Zoroastrian beliefs. So Jesus and the twenty-four spent much of their time making plain the difference between these older beliefs and the new gospel of the kingdom. Many believed, but it is difficult to bring nature worshipers into the full fellowship of a spiritual ideal within a single lifetime.
146.b9.p: The paper adds that many of the better Babylonian and Persian ideas later entered the doctrines of Christianity and made them more acceptable to the peoples of the Near East, while Plato’s theories, adapted by Philo, made Paul’s teachings easier for the western Greeks to accept. It was at Rimmon that Todan first heard the gospel; he later carried it into Mesopotamia and far beyond the Euphrates.
146.b11.p: At Jotapata Nathaniel was confused about the Master’s teaching on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship, and in answer Jesus gave the twenty-four a long discourse. Harboring iniquity in the heart gradually destroys the prayer connection with God, and the prayer of one who disdains the divine laws becomes an abomination. The Father has forgiven us even before we ask, but that forgiveness becomes real in our experience only when we forgive our fellows.
146.b12.t: Deliberate iniquity cuts the spirit circuits of prayer
God’s forgiveness is experienced as we forgive others
Even infinite love cannot force survival on one who will not choose it
With the spirit with which you judge, you will be judged
A prayer in full accord with his will is surely answered
Pray more for the spiritual progress of your brethren
Prayer cannot take the place of loving ministry to the sick
Praying only in trouble is thoughtless
Thanksgiving leads to worship; after praying, wait in silence
146.b13.p: Prayer, Jesus said, is not a way to escape the delays of time or the handicaps of space, nor a technique for gaining advantage over others. It is the motive of the prayer that gives it right of way to the divine ear, not the status of the one who prays. And there is only one form of prayer fitting for all God’s children: “⟦Q 146:2.12⟧Nevertheless, your will be done.⟦/Q⟧”
146.b14.q: ⟦Q 146:2.17⟧Worship is a transforming experience whereby the finite gradually approaches and ultimately attains the presence of the Infinite.⟦/Q⟧
146.b16.p: At Ramah Jesus listened with patience and sympathy to an aged Greek philosopher who taught that science and philosophy were enough, and he granted the truth of much that the man said. But he pointed out that the philosopher had failed to explain “⟦Q 146:3.1⟧whence, why, and whither,⟦/Q⟧” and added, “⟦Q 146:3.1⟧Where you leave off, we begin.⟦/Q⟧” The old man soon believed. When the apostles were disconcerted, Jesus taught them that true inward certainty does not fear outward analysis.
146.b17.q: ⟦Q 146:3.2⟧intolerance is the mask covering up the entertainment of secret doubts as to the trueness of one’s belief.⟦/Q⟧
146.b18.p: When Thomas asked how a new believer could be sure of the truth of the gospel, Jesus answered that such assurance is wholly a matter of personal experience. We cannot watch the divine spirit at work in our minds, but there is a practical way to discover how far we have yielded to its guidance: the degree of our love for our fellow men.
146.b19.t: Personal religious experience in the eternal realities of divine truth
146.b20.p: At Zebulun, in one of the few times he ever did so, Jesus discussed the social side of religion — the difference between personal religious experience and the obligations of social religion. From this time on each of Jesus’ apostles had one of John’s apostles as an associate.
146.b22.p: At this time every synagogue in Galilee and Judea was still open to Jesus. In the mining town of Iron he spent most of his time working in the mines with the underground laborers while the apostles preached. On the third day a leper knelt before him and said, “⟦Q 146:4.3⟧Lord, if only you would, you could make me clean.⟦/Q⟧” Moved with compassion, Jesus touched him and said, “⟦Q 146:4.3⟧I will—be clean,⟦/Q⟧” and he was healed at once.
146.b23.p: This was the first so-called miracle Jesus had intentionally performed, and it was a case of real leprosy. But the man ignored Jesus’ charge to tell no one and spread the news everywhere, so that Jesus had to leave the village the next day. At Chorazin and Madon the message met with wide rejection. Most of the apostles blamed this on Jesus’ refusal to let them speak of him as a healer, but the Master was unmoved.
146.b25.p: At Cana Titus, a prominent citizen of Capernaum, begged Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus lamented that people would not believe unless they saw signs, but after a moment of silent meditation he said, “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧Return to your home; your son will live.⟦/Q⟧” The boy’s fever left him at that very hour, and Titus and his whole family believed.
146.b26.p: The paper explains that this was not a miracle of curing disease; it was a case of preknowledge concerning the course of natural law. But people believed he had healed from a distance and began sending messengers asking him to do the same, and once more Jesus had to hurry away from Cana.
146.b28.p: The Galileans expected wonders, and they took every recovery from nervous or emotional disorders for a miraculous physical cure. At the gate of Nain Jesus met the funeral procession of a widow’s only son. Finding that the boy was not really dead, he said to the mother, “⟦Q 146:6.2⟧Weep not. Your son is not dead; he sleeps,⟦/Q⟧” and then told the young man, “⟦Q 146:6.2|146:6.4|152:1.1⟧Awake and arise.⟦/Q⟧”
146.b29.p: Jesus tried again and again to explain that the boy had not been dead, but the people took his words as modesty hiding a miracle, and the report that he had raised the dead spread through Galilee and Judea. Not even his apostles fully understood.
146.b30.t: A healing miracle done at a distance
Preknowledge of the course of natural law
A miracle of raising the dead
The boy was not dead but in a deep sleep
The first so-called miracle Jesus intentionally performed
146.b32.p: Resting at Endor away from the crowds, Jesus told the apostles the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor. The so-called spirits of the dead, he explained, had often been stray and rebellious midwayers impersonating them, and after he returned to the Father and the spirit was poured out upon all flesh, such beings could no longer possess the minds of men. The spirits of departed human beings do not come back to their native world to communicate with the living. After two days Jesus said they would return to Capernaum.
146.b34.p: The journey of Paper 146 runs along two lines. On one side, people expected miracles everywhere, turning coincidence and foreknowledge alike into wonders, and Jesus had to leave town after town to escape the uproar. On the other, Jesus quietly taught the deepest things: that prayer changes not the Father but us, that spiritual assurance comes from personal experience, and that how far we have yielded to the spirit shows in how much we love our neighbors. Signs left rumors behind; truth changed souls.
146.b35.t: He made plain the difference between old nature worship and the new gospel
Prayer changes not the Father’s attitude but ours
Assurance comes from experience, and love for others is its proof
The cleansing of the leper was the first intentional miracle
The healing of Titus’ son was not a miracle but foreknowledge
He woke a sleeping boy, but people believed he had raised the dead
The spirits of the dead do not return to communicate with the living
146.b37.box: Miracles leave only rumors behind, but truth experienced through prayer and love changes the soul.
147.title: The Interlude Visit to Jerusalem
147.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus measure a person’s worth not by where they stand today but by the direction they move each day?”
147.b2.p: In Paper 146 Jesus and the apostles finished their first preaching tour of Galilee and returned to Capernaum on March 17, A.D. 28. Paper 147 records the short interlude that followed, a trip to Jerusalem for the Passover. For two weeks the apostles taught by the seaside, while Jesus, with James and John, made two secret trips to Tiberias to instruct believers from Herod’s household.
147.b3.p: These believers explained to Herod that the kingdom Jesus proclaimed was spiritual, not political, and Herod raised no objection to his work. The greater danger to Jesus lay not in Herod but in the religious leaders at Jerusalem, and that is why he did most of his public preaching in Galilee.
147.b4.p: This paper brings us a gentile centurion’s faith, words of comfort at the pool of Bethesda, six levels of the golden rule, a woman who entered the house of Simon the Pharisee, and disputes over the Sabbath and fasting. In these encounters, where did Jesus see a person’s true worth?
147.b5.q: “⟦Q 147:5.7⟧What you are becoming day by day is of infinitely more importance than what you are today.⟦/Q⟧”
147.b8.p: The day before they set out for the Passover, Mangus, a Roman centurion at Capernaum, sent Jewish elders to ask Jesus to heal his servant, who was near death. The elders said he loved their nation and had even built their synagogue. As Jesus went with them, the centurion sent friends to say that he was not worthy to have the Master under his roof; Jesus had only to speak the word, and his servant would be healed.
147.b9.p: Jesus said, “⟦Q 147:1.3⟧I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel,⟦/Q⟧” and turned away. From that hour the servant began to mend. The paper records honestly that it was never revealed whether invisible beings ministered healing; we know only that the servant fully recovered.
147.b11.p: Leaving on March 30 by way of the Jordan valley, the party reached Bethany on April 2. Passing through Jericho, Judas for the first time deposited some of their surplus funds in a bank. So many came seeking healing and comfort that Jesus went back and forth between Bethany and Gethsemane, and for nearly three weeks he allowed no public preaching, only private teaching and personal work.
147.b12.p: At Bethany they quietly celebrated the bloodless Passover, while John’s apostles kept the feast separately with Abner. Afterward John’s apostles stayed on to work in and around Jerusalem; the two groups worked apart but cooperated, and the best of feelings prevailed.
147.b14.p: On the second Sabbath in Jerusalem, John took Jesus to the pool of Bethesda, a hot spring that bubbled up now and then from gas below. People believed that the first one into the water after it stirred would be healed. John hoped a miracle there would win all Jerusalem, but Jesus answered, “⟦Q 147:3.2⟧John, why would you tempt me to turn aside from the way I have chosen?⟦/Q⟧” and offered words of comfort instead.
147.b15.p: He told the sufferers that their afflictions came from many causes — wrong living, accidents, the mistakes of their forebears — but that all of them were God’s children and that the God of eternity loved them. One man, who for years had been gripped by helplessness and had waited for someone else to help him, rejoiced at these words, picked up his bed, and walked home. Helping himself was the one thing he had needed to do.
147.b17.p: That evening Nathaniel asked how the rule “do to others as you wish them to do to you” could apply to a lustful man who might twist it. Jesus replied that he had spoken to men of high ideals, and then taught six levels of meaning in this rule of living. Nothing he had said up to that time ever astonished the apostles more.
147.b18.t: How the golden rule is read
A purely selfish and lustful reading
Raised a step by sympathy and pity
Reason, experience, and the ideal of profound self-respect
Unselfish devotion to the welfare of others
As a wise and impartial third person would see it
Treat all men as God would treat them
147.b19.q: “⟦Q 147:4.9⟧I would, therefore, that you should do to all men that which you know I would do to them in like circumstances.⟦/Q⟧”
147.b21.p: When Simon, an influential Pharisee, invited Jesus to a meal, a woman came in from the street, wet his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them. She had believed the gospel, closed her evil business, and led most of the women with her into a new life, yet she was still scorned. When Simon judged her in his heart, Jesus told the parable of the two debtors whose debts were forgiven.
147.b22.t: Washed them with tears and wiped them with her hair
Has not ceased to kiss his feet
Did not anoint his head with oil
Anointed his feet with precious lotions
147.b23.p: Those forgiven much love much, Jesus said, and he told the woman, “⟦Q 147:5.5⟧Go in peace; your faith has saved you.⟦/Q⟧” To Simon he said he prayed that he too would experience such a transformation. That evening he taught the apostles that the certainty of progress matters more than its speed, and the Godward direction of progress more than present achievement. A small but living and growing faith is far better than a great intellect with its dead stores of spiritual unbelief.
147.b24.p: At the same time Jesus earnestly warned them not to mistake the Father for a lax or foolishly indulgent parent ready to excuse sin. The Father does not condone the practices of his children that are self-destructive to moral growth and spiritual progress.
147.b26.p: The leaders at Jerusalem decided that Jesus must be arrested on a religious charge and tried by the Sanhedrin, and they sent six secret spies who joined the party pretending to be disciples. When the group set out on a Sabbath morning, Jesus had Andrew lead them only the legal Sabbath day’s journey, and the spies’ first charge came to nothing.
147.b27.p: But when the apostles plucked and rubbed grain in the fields, the spies protested that they were breaking the Sabbath. Jesus reminded them how the hungry David ate the showbread and told them that guarding the health and well-being of their fellows was better than zeal for the Sabbath. His opposition to tradition was always positive, consisting in what he did and affirmed rather than in denunciation.
147.b28.q: “⟦Q 147:6.4⟧the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath.⟦/Q⟧”
147.b30.p: Back in Bethsaida on May 3, the leader of the spies asked why Jesus never commanded his disciples to fast. Jesus answered that the sons of the bridechamber do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, and that fasting is not a part of the gospel of the kingdom. No one sews new cloth on an old garment or puts new wine into old skins; likewise his disciples were wise not to bring too much of the old order into the new teaching.
147.b31.t: Have the faith and courage to accept it
147.b33.p: That night Jesus taught the true fast in the words of Isaiah. The fast God chooses is not a day to afflict one’s soul but to loose the bonds of wickedness, let the oppressed go free, and share one’s bread with the hungry. Until after two in the morning he taught that it was their faith, not affliction of soul or fasting of body, that made them secure in the kingdom.
147.b34.p: His last words that night were these: “⟦Q 147:8.5⟧Grow in grace by means of that living faith which grasps the fact that you are the sons of God while at the same time it recognizes every man as a brother.⟦/Q⟧”
147.b36.p: The brief Jerusalem visit of Paper 147 shows how Jesus looked at people. In a gentile centurion he saw faith not found even in Israel; in a man trapped by helplessness he awakened the power to rise on his own; in a woman everyone despised he saw a soul moving toward God ahead of the Pharisee. He unfolded the golden rule on six levels, ending with treating others as God would treat them, and he placed human well-being and faith above the rules of Sabbath and fasting. What mattered to Jesus was not where a person stood today but a living faith moving Godward day by day.
147.b37.t: He found in a gentile centurion faith not found even in Israel
They quietly kept the bloodless Passover and taught in private
With comfort instead of a miracle, he helped a man rise on his own
The golden rule at its highest means treating others as God would
Those forgiven much love much, and direction is what matters
The Sabbath was made for man
New wine in fresh skins; keep what is true, old or new
The true fast frees the oppressed and shares bread with the hungry
147.b39.q: ⟦Q 147:5.7⟧The important thing is not the rapidity of your progress but rather its certainty. Your actual achievement is not so important as the fact that the direction of your progress is Godward.⟦/Q⟧
148.title: Training Evangelists at Bethsaida
148.b0.ask: “If we have a loving Father, why do people suffer — and how is evil different from sin?”
148.b2.p: In Paper 147 Jesus and the apostles returned from Jerusalem to Bethsaida on May 3, A.D. 28. Paper 148 covers the five months from that day to October 3, spent by the seaside near the Zebedee home — the longest settled and well-organized period of the Master’s teaching. A tented city of five hundred to fifteen hundred people grew up there. David Zebedee ran it as a self-sustaining enterprise, and it was a model of order and sanitation.
148.b3.p: Andrew remained in general charge of the apostolic work, while Peter took full charge of the school of evangelists. In the mornings the apostles taught the evangelists; in the afternoons teachers and pupils taught the people together; and once a week Jesus presided over the question hour.
148.b4.p: In this quiet season Jesus shared the deepest questions with his apostles in the garden. What is evil? And why do people suffer under a loving Father?
148.b5.q: “⟦Q 148:6.10⟧God dwells within you, that he has become what you are that he may make you what he is!⟦/Q⟧”
148.b7.h: 1. A New School of the Prophets
148.b8.p: Peter, James, and Andrew passed on the applicants, and the students represented every race and nation of the Roman world and the East, as far as India. The school ran on the plan of learning and doing: what the students learned in the morning they taught by the seaside in the afternoon, and after supper they discussed both together.
148.b9.p: Each apostle taught the gospel from his own point of view; there was no effort to make them teach alike and no fixed creed. Jesus upheld this diversity of personal experience and harmonized the different views at his weekly question hours. The hundred and more evangelists trained here became the core from which the seventy were later drawn.
148.b11.p: Elman, a Syrian physician, assisted by twenty-five young women and twelve men, ran for four months what should be regarded as the kingdom’s first hospital. They treated the sick by all known material methods as well as by prayer and faith encouragement, and Jesus visited the sick at least three times a week, meeting each sufferer personally.
148.b12.p: Among the thousand who left improved or cured, there was no supernatural miracle, yet most of them proclaimed that Jesus had healed them. The paper explains these cures as transformations of mind and spirit in expectant, faith-filled people under the influence of a strong and kindly personality whose ministry banished fear.
148.b14.p: During this time Jesus led public services at the camp fewer than a dozen times, and never since his baptism had he been so much alone. Whenever someone asked why he was away so often, he answered that he was “⟦Q 148:3.2|148:3.3|148:7.1⟧about the Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧” He took along any two apostles who were free, so that each of the twelve had a chance for close fellowship with him.
148.b15.p: The writers carefully note that they infer, though it was not revealed, that in these hours Jesus was directing phases of universe administration in association with his chief directors of universe affairs. The apostles near him saw his face change many times, though they heard no words.
148.b17.p: In a private talk in the garden, Thomas asked why people must be born of the spirit and what evil is. Jesus first told him not to confuse evil with the evil one — the high administrator who knowingly rebelled, and whom Jesus had already vanquished. Then he set out three ways of relating to the Father’s will.
148.b18.t: How the Father’s will is transgressed
The continued rejection of the Father’s loving plan of survival
148.b19.p: Before the rebirth of the spirit, man is subject to inherent evil tendencies, but such natural imperfections are neither sin nor iniquity. Correcting the idea that mankind fell from a perfect Adam, Jesus taught that man, by entering the kingdom, is ascending surely up to God and divine perfection.
148.b20.q: “⟦Q 148:4.8⟧Men are, indeed, by nature evil, but not necessarily sinful.⟦/Q⟧”
148.b22.p: Nathaniel asked why the loving Father allows his children to suffer so many afflictions. Jesus answered that the natural order of this world had been upset many times by the sinful adventures of rebels, and that many ages would be needed to set it right. The Father does not purposely afflict his children, nor does he send affliction as an arbitrary punishment for wrongdoing.
148.b24.p: Man should not blame God for the natural results of the life he chooses; the Father’s will is that we work persistently to better our estate on earth. Do not ascribe to God everything you fail to understand, Jesus said, and then he recited many passages of Scripture that offer comfort in affliction.
148.b25.h: 6. The Misunderstanding of Suffering—Discourse on Job
148.b26.p: That same evening John asked why so many apparently innocent people suffer, and Jesus explained the Book of Job. Material prosperity is no proof of God’s favor; the Father loves the poor just as much as the rich. People do reap what they sow, but human suffering is not always a punishment for past sin.
148.b27.t: It is the wicked who suffer; you must deserve this
Your children perished, so they must have been sinners
God’s ways cannot be understood; perhaps there is a hidden purpose
148.b28.p: Disgusted with his friends, Job appealed to a just God against the God of injustice in their philosophy, and at last cried out in triumph, “⟦Q 148:6.9⟧My Vindicator lives!⟦/Q⟧” What Job longed for was a God who understands man’s mortal estate, and the Son of Man came in the flesh to comfort all who must endure such afflictions. God speaks not from the whirlwind but within the heart as a still, small voice: “⟦Q 148:6.10⟧This is the way; walk therein.⟦/Q⟧”
148.b29.t: The accidents of time and the imperfections of an immature physical existence
The inexorable consequences of sin, the transgression of the laws of life and light
The harvest of his own persistence in rebellion against the rule of heaven
148.b30.p: Yet man’s miseries are not a personal visitation of divine judgment, and we must be delivered once and for all from the superstition that God afflicts man at the behest of the evil one. This conversation markedly changed John’s whole life.
148.b31.h: 7. The Man with the Withered Hand
148.b32.p: On a Sabbath shortly before the second preaching tour, the leader of the Jerusalem spies sent a man with a withered hand to Jesus in the Capernaum synagogue. Jesus asked whether one would lift a sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath, declared that a man is far more valuable than a sheep and that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, and told the man to stretch out his hand. It was made whole.
148.b33.p: This was the first miracle Jesus worked in response to a challenge from his enemies, done not to display his power but as a protest against turning the Sabbath into a bondage of meaningless restrictions. The angry Pharisees went to Herod, but Herod refused to act against Jesus.
148.b35.p: In the last week three of the spies were deeply impressed, and in Jerusalem Abraham, a young member of the Sanhedrin, openly espoused Jesus’ teachings and was baptized. He gave all his worldly goods to the apostolic treasury, which made it possible to send out the hundred new evangelists at once.
148.b36.p: Visitors from Alexandria again invited Jesus to found a school and an infirmary there, but he courteously declined. When Kirmeth, a self-styled prophet from Bagdad, came to the camp, Jesus allowed him complete freedom for a few days, and those who heard him soon saw for themselves that his teaching was not sound.
148.b38.p: At the last meeting on October 1, the Zebedee house was so crowded that a paralytic from Capernaum had his friends remove the roof tiles and lower him on his couch right in front of Jesus. He said he wanted to be made whole, not like those who were healed and forgot the teaching, but in order to serve in the kingdom. Seeing his faith, Jesus said, “⟦Q 148:9.2⟧Son, fear not; your sins are forgiven.⟦/Q⟧”
148.b39.p: When the Pharisees inwardly charged him with blasphemy, Jesus said that they might know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and told the man, “⟦Q 148:9.3⟧Arise, take up your bed, and go to your own house.⟦/Q⟧” He got up and walked out before them all. Just then the summons from the Sanhedrin arrived; three of the spies went back, but the other three confessed faith in Jesus and were baptized by Peter.
148.b41.p: Paper 148 shows five months of learning and caring in a tented city by the sea. The evangelists grew by learning and teaching, and at the first hospital medicine and faith worked together for the sick. In the midst of it all Jesus answered the hardest questions. Evil is imperfection, not sin, and man is not a fallen creature sliding downward but one ascending toward God. Suffering is not a penalty the Father sends but the result of imperfection, sin, and rebellion; and when faith pierces those clouds, as Job’s did, we find the God of comfort and salvation. God became what we are so that he might make us what he is.
148.b42.t: Section
Key message
A New School of the Prophets
Evangelists were trained by learning and doing, with differing views harmonized
The Bethsaida Hospital
The first hospital joined medicine and faith — and worked no miracles
The Father’s Business
Jesus attended to universe affairs alone, taking two apostles with him
Evil, Sin, and Iniquity
Evil is imperfection, sin is deliberate, iniquity is persistent rejection
The Purpose of Affliction
The Father does not send affliction as punishment
The Misunderstanding of Suffering—Discourse on Job
Even in suffering, faith finds the God of comfort and salvation
The Man with the Withered Hand
It is lawful to do good to men on the Sabbath
Last Week at Bethsaida
The spies divided, and a convert’s gift opened the way for the evangelists
Healing the Paralytic
The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
148.b44.q: ⟦Q 148:6.11⟧The Father in heaven does not willingly afflict the children of men.⟦/Q⟧
149.title: The Second Preaching Tour
149.b0.ask: “Before crowds that came looking for miracles, why did Jesus teach them to approach God in love rather than in fear?”
149.b2.p: If the school at the Bethsaida camp in Paper 148 trained 117 new workers, Paper 149 tells of their first time in the field. The second public preaching tour of Galilee began on October 3, A.D. 28, and lasted almost three months, until December 30.
149.b3.p: Jesus declined to give the final charge to the new evangelists, saying it was not his province to do what others could acceptably do, so James Zebedee gave it instead. On this tour only James and John traveled with Jesus, sometimes visiting two cities in a day, while each of the other apostles took about a dozen evangelists with him. The whole tour was meant chiefly to give the new corps practical experience. At the Zebedee home in Bethsaida, David Zebedee kept a clearinghouse for the work, with forty to fifty messengers.
149.b4.p: As his fame as a healer spread, Jesus wanted people to come to God through him, not through miracles. What is the path from a religion of fear to a religion of love?
149.b5.q: ⟦Q 149:2.7⟧Learn to approach the miracle through Jesus, but do not make the mistake of approaching Jesus through the miracle.⟦/Q⟧
149.b8.p: By the time the Bethsaida camp broke up, Jesus’ fame as a healer had spread through Palestine, Syria, and the surrounding countries. On this tour he did not deliberately perform any so-called miracles of healing, yet many regained their health through the power of their intense faith. In three months more than a hundred people from many regions received this unconscious healing from Jesus, and although he told them to “⟦Q 149:1.2|129:2.10|136:8.1⟧tell no man,⟦/Q⟧” they spread his fame still further.
149.b9.p: Jesus never explained how these healings happened; several times he said only, “⟦Q 149:1.3⟧I perceive that power has gone forth from me.⟦/Q⟧” The writers carefully offer their own opinion: many of these apparent miracles resulted from three associated influences acting together.
149.b10.t: A strong, living faith that sought healing for its spiritual benefits
The great sympathy of the Creator Son, who held creative healing powers
Unless the Father willed otherwise, the need and the power became one
149.b11.p: The explanation must be found in a great law: what the Creator Son desires and the eternal Father wills is. Jesus often let people heal themselves in his presence by their powerful faith. Others, like a rich widow of Tyre, acted as if the power of God could be bought, caring nothing for the gospel and seeking only the cure of their bodies.
149.b13.p: Had Jesus’ teachings been left as he presented them, all nations and religions would soon have embraced the gospel. But his early followers, meaning well, restated his teachings to suit certain groups, and that only made them less acceptable to everyone else. Christianity contains more of the Master’s gospel than any other religion, yet it also contains much that Jesus did not teach, and the paper names two great mistakes.
149.b14.t: 1. Connecting the gospel to Jewish theology
The doctrine of atonement — a sacrifice to appease divine wrath — which alienated many honest souls
2. Organizing the teaching completely about the person of Jesus
His person came to obscure his teachings, making them harder for Eastern religionists to accept
149.b15.p: His saving message is the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Teachers of his religion should approach other religions by recognizing the truths they hold in common rather than stressing differences. With the Creator himself on earth, extraordinary things were bound to happen — but we should approach the miracle through Jesus, not Jesus through the miracle.
149.b16.p: The most revolutionary feature of his mission was his attitude toward women. In an age when a man would not greet even his own wife in public, Jesus took women along as teachers of the gospel, and in one generation he lifted women out of disrespect and drudgery. He was free from the superstitions of his day, taught that calamities are not divine judgments, and made clean hearts rather than clean hands the mark of true religion.
149.b17.q: ⟦Q 149:2.11⟧He was not a militant revolutionist; he was a progressive evolutionist.⟦/Q⟧
149.b18.p: He tore down what was only when he offered something better in its place. He did not demand obedience, yet he inspired confidence. Only those who had not met him feared him. The better people knew him, the more they loved him — and that is still true today.
149.b20.p: While the common people welcomed Jesus, the religious leaders at Jerusalem grew more and more hostile. The Pharisees had built a systematic theology, but Jesus taught as the occasion served, from life and by parables. A parable was meant to illustrate one feature only; turning his parables into allegories breeds many wrong ideas.
149.b21.p: The conversion of young Abraham and the desertion of the three spies left the leaders almost frantic, and their hearts hardened as they kept rejecting the truth. Jesus had said that the only uniform thing about men is the indwelling spirit, and that only by appeal to this spirit can mankind reach unity and brotherhood. But from this time on the leaders never stopped plotting his destruction.
149.b23.p: Jesus did little public work on this tour but held many evening classes with believers. Asked about anger, he said it measures the failure of the spiritual nature to control the intellectual and physical natures, and reveals a lack of brotherly love and self-control. Anger depletes the health, debases the mind, and handicaps the spirit teacher of the soul.
149.b24.p: On the same occasion he spoke of the value of a well-balanced character, pointing out that any virtue carried to extremes may become a vice.
149.b26.p: He asked for originality without eccentricity, sympathy without sentimentality, piety without sanctimoniousness, and reverence free from fear and superstition. What impressed his associates was less his teaching than the way his own life embodied it. He lived amid stress and storm yet never wavered, and he never stooped to ignoble tactics. Even while devoted to a vocation, people should cultivate a wide familiarity with life as a whole.
149.b28.p: Simon Zelotes asked why some people are happier and more contented than others. Jesus answered that some are naturally happier, but that much depends on one’s willingness to be led by the Father’s indwelling spirit, and he quoted Scriptures about the righteous man who is content with little.
149.b29.p: Much of our sorrow comes from disappointed ambition and wounded pride. After sincerely doing our best, we should cheerfully accept our lot and use ingenuity to make the most of it. Seek not false peace and passing joy but the assurance of faith and the sureties of divine sonship, which bring composure and contentment. Jesus did not see this world as a “⟦Q 149:5.5|40:7.5⟧vale of tears⟦/Q⟧” but as the “⟦Q 149:5.5⟧vale of soul making.⟦/Q⟧”
149.b31.p: At Gamala Philip asked how the Scriptures’ command to “⟦Q 149:6.1⟧fear the Lord⟦/Q⟧” could be reconciled with Jesus’ teaching to look to the Father without fear. Jesus answered that in the beginning man could learn reverence only through fear, but he had come to reveal the Father’s love. The “⟦Q 149:6.3|149:6.5|68:3.3⟧fear of the Lord⟦/Q⟧” had meant different things in different ages.
149.b32.t: When man sees only the works and power of God
When man begins to experience God’s character and personality
Where the Son of Man would lead us
149.b33.p: The goodness of God leads to repentance, his beneficence to service, his mercy to salvation, and his love to intelligent and freehearted worship. Our forebears feared God because he was mighty and mysterious; we adore him because he is magnificent in love and plenteous in mercy. In the kingdom of heaven there is no high and mighty king; the kingdom is a divine family.
149.b34.t: Fear God and keep his commandments
Love God and learn to do his will
149.b35.q: “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧I have come into the world to put love in the place of fear, joy in the place of sorrow, confidence in the place of dread⟦/Q⟧”
149.b36.p: False ideas of humility and much hypocrisy grow out of wrong concepts of the Father. Man may be a worm of the dust by nature, but when the Father’s spirit dwells in him, he becomes divine in destiny. Humility before God and meekness before men are good, but attention-craving humility is childish. The Father disdains pride and loathes hypocrisy, and he dwells with the one who has a contrite mind and a humble spirit.
149.b38.p: With Jesus’ approval, Andrew had David call all the groups back to Bethsaida by December 30. They spent the Sabbath together and were then given a two weeks’ recess; even the older teachers were edified by the young evangelists’ accounts of their experiences.
149.b39.p: Of the 117 evangelists, only about seventy-five survived the test of actual experience and were ready to continue in service. Jesus remained at the Zebedee home with Andrew, Peter, James, and John, conferring on the extension of the kingdom.
149.b41.p: Paper 149 records three months in which Jesus, famed as a healer, tried to turn people’s eyes from miracles to God. He deliberately worked no miracles, made women teachers of the gospel, and showed in his own life a balance that guarded against anger and extremes. At the center of all his teaching lay his mission to change man’s relation to God from fear to love. God is not a king to be feared but a Father to be loved, and the kingdom of heaven is a divine family with him at its head. Like the seventy-five evangelists who remained after the test of real experience, this teaching is proved and grows in actual living.
149.b42.t: Healing came where faith, the Creator’s compassion, and the Father’s will met
Approach the miracle through Jesus, not Jesus through the miracle
Leaders who shut out the spirit’s appeal hardened their hearts
Any virtue carried to extremes becomes a vice; keep a balance
Contentment comes from willingness to be spirit-led and the assurance of faith
Do not fear God as a king; love him as a Father
Of 117 evangelists, about seventy-five passed the test of experience
149.b44.q: ⟦Q 149:6.3⟧it is just this changing of the relation of man to God that constitutes the mission of the Son of Man on earth.⟦/Q⟧
